rows.title: Wegovy cost in the UK: look beyond the first pen
rows.author: Matt O’Brien
rows.summary: Understand Wegovy costs in the UK, compare four-week quotes fairly, check safe supply and plan for support during treatment and after it ends.
rows.body:
# Wegovy cost in the UK: look beyond the first pen

The price matters. So does knowing what happens after the delivery turns up. Here is how to compare the full cost, check who is looking after you and plan for the support you want around treatment.

![Three men standing together with their arms around one another](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/assets/home-hero-men-v32o.jpg?v=42g3)

*Support that fits around real life. SHIFT brand imagery.*

If you are weighing up Wegovy, you probably have a fairly ordinary question: can I afford this without making the rest of life harder?

That deserves a straight answer. There is no single UK private price. Your prescribed dose, the amount supplied and what the service includes all affect the bill. An introductory offer tells you little about what you will pay later.

For most blokes, this is about more than buying a pen. It might be feeling comfortable in your clothes, getting back to football or having more energy for a family day out. The budget needs to make sense alongside those reasons.

## The quick answer

- **Compare the same dose and supply period.** Four weeks and a calendar month are different.
- **Ask for the full bill.** Include any consultation, review, delivery and membership charges that actually apply.
- **Check the provider, not just the price.** A lower price is not proof of a fake; a higher price is not proof of good care.
- **Ask what support continues.** Know who handles medicine questions and what help remains if treatment changes or stops.

Wegovy is a prescription medicine. Whether it is appropriate for you, and which dose to use, are decisions for a qualified prescriber. The [NHS semaglutide guide](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/semaglutide/) explains the basics and the importance of using a registered pharmacy.

## How much does Wegovy cost over a year?

Start with a current quote for the dose you have been prescribed. Then check how many weeks that quote covers. Private prices can change, so a dated quote is more useful than a headline range copied around the internet.

**A four-week price needs 13 payments to cover 52 weeks.** Multiplying it by 12 only covers 48 weeks. A calendar year is slightly longer than 52 weeks, so check your actual supply dates too.

These examples show the arithmetic. They are **not current pharmacy quotes, SHIFT prices or a recommendation to take treatment for a year**.

| Example price for four weeks | Four-week supplies in 52 weeks | Medication total for 52 weeks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| £150 | 13 | £1,950 |
| £200 | 13 | £2,600 |
| £250 | 13 | £3,250 |

![Illustrative four-week quotes of £150, £200 and £250 total £1,950, £2,600 and £3,250 over 52 weeks](/assets/articles/wegovy-cost-uk/annual-budget.svg)

*Illustrative arithmetic: 13 four-week supplies cover 52 weeks. These are not current pharmacy quotes or SHIFT prices.*

If your quote is genuinely per calendar month, use its monthly billing terms instead. If the dose or price changes, add the actual supplies at each price rather than applying one starter offer to the whole year.

Your first year may include different doses and periods without treatment. Ask your prescriber and provider what to expect; do not pick a dose to fit an online cost table. The [UK product information](https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/13803/smpc) sets out the dosing framework, while individual treatment decisions belong with your prescriber.

### What else belongs in the budget?

Ask whether the quoted fee includes:

- the initial assessment and prescribing decision;
- follow-up reviews and a route for medicine questions;
- delivery and any charge for a replacement or missed delivery;
- tests, if your clinician says they are needed;
- a compulsory membership or subscription;
- any change in price when an introductory offer ends.

Do not add a made-up allowance for blood tests or assume every service charges extra. Ask what applies to your situation, get it in writing and compare the total on the same basis.

If the continuing cost looks difficult, say so before starting. A treatment plan needs to fit your circumstances. Do not stretch doses, share pens or change treatment to make an offer last longer; discuss affordability and alternatives with your prescriber.

## Can you get Wegovy on the NHS?

Wegovy can be prescribed through the NHS when the relevant criteria and local pathway are met. NHS access is not the same as meeting a medicine's licensed eligibility criteria. Ask your GP or local weight-management service what is available and how referrals work in your area. The [NHS information on semaglutide](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/semaglutide/) describes specialist assessment for weight management.

An NHS prescription is different from a private quote. Where an NHS prescription charge applies in England, the current standard charge is **£9.90 per item**, with exemptions and prepayment arrangements available. That is not a private Wegovy price or a promise of NHS access. Check the [current NHS prescription-charge guidance](https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/prescriptions/nhs-prescription-charges/).

You can also ask about support that does not depend on obtaining a prescription. The [NHS weight-management information](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/overweight-and-obesity/) covers programmes, lifestyle support and treatment routes.

## How do you check that an online provider is legitimate?

A convincing website and a low price are not enough. Equally, an expensive quote does not tell you how good the service is.

Before paying, get clear answers to four questions:

1. **Who assesses and prescribes?** Get the clinician's name and professional registration details. Check those details with the relevant regulator.
2. **Which pharmacy supplies the medicine?** Match its name and address against the appropriate pharmacy register. For a pharmacy in Great Britain, check the General Pharmaceutical Council; Northern Ireland has a separate pharmacy regulator.
3. **Who helps if something goes wrong?** Know how to contact the prescriber, pharmacist and customer-support team, and what each can help with.
4. **How is the medicine delivered and stored?** Ask about packaging, delays and what to do if a delivery arrives in an unexpected condition. Follow the instructions supplied with your medicine and contact the pharmacy if you are unsure.

The [NHS warns that some websites sell fake weight-loss medicines](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/semaglutide/). Use a registered pharmacy and a proper prescription route. Do not treat price alone as a test of authenticity.

One outdated tip still circulates: that every UK seller must display the distance-selling logo. The [MHRA says that requirement ended in Great Britain in January 2021](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/register-for-the-distance-selling-logo); requirements continue in Northern Ireland. Verify the actual business rather than relying on a badge.

## What should useful support look like?

Before you join a service, ask what happens after the first prescription:

- How do I ask about side effects or a missed dose?
- Who decides whether my dose changes?
- When is my next review, and what does it cost?
- What happens if supply is interrupted or I need to change provider?
- What is the plan if treatment is no longer suitable or affordable?
- What support remains when treatment stops?

Clear answers matter more than a vague promise of unlimited support. A delivery update, a wellbeing check-in and a clinical review are different things. You should know which you are receiving.

Weight-management support also has to fit around normal life: meals after work, movement you can repeat, sleep, confidence and the days when motivation disappears. The [NHS describes medicines alongside diet and lifestyle advice, with support after stopping](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/overweight-and-obesity/).

![Four checks: the full bill, the named prescriber and pharmacy, help when needed, and support if treatment changes or stops](/assets/articles/wegovy-cost-uk/provider-checklist.svg)

*Compare the service around the medicine as well as the price.*

## Where SHIFT fits into the picture

SHIFT brings treatment information and practical support together around a simple question: **what do you want your life back for?**

Your medicine is one part of that picture. You still need dinner on a busy Wednesday. You still need a way to get moving that fits your starting point. And you deserve to notice progress beyond a single weigh-in.

| Part of SHIFT | What it helps you do |
| --- | --- |
| [Grub](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/member/grub) | Find food ideas and make the next meal easier to plan. |
| [Fit](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/member/fit) | Explore movement options that suit your circumstances. |
| [My Timber](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/member/dashboard) | Keep your goals, check-ins and progress together. |
| [Life Back](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/life-back) | Record the everyday things you want to get back to: energy, confidence, clothes, hobbies or family life. |
| [Continuity](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/stopping-glp1) | Understand the questions and practical planning around changing or stopping treatment. |

You can explore the [Programme](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/programme) whether you are considering treatment, already taking it elsewhere or planning your next stage. Member tools may require sign-in. Medicine decisions and clinical follow-up remain with your prescriber; a My Timber check-in is not a clinical review.

For treatment routes, use [Treatments](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/treatment-centre) and check the current product information and availability. **“No stock available today” means exactly that.** Reading this guide does not reserve medication or guarantee that a prescription will be suitable.

If food thoughts are taking up more headspace after treatment changes, our [food-noise guide](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/food-noise-after-stopping-glp1) is a useful next read. Persistent or worrying symptoms need a conversation with a healthcare professional.

## Before you decide: three useful next steps

1. **Get one complete quote.** Same dose, same supply period, all required fees included.
2. **Write down who does what.** Prescriber, pharmacy, support contact and the next review.
3. **Choose one everyday goal.** Something you want to do or feel more comfortable doing, alongside any weight goal.

You do not need to solve the whole year tonight. Get the facts straight, make the next decision with your eyes open and keep the reason you started in view.

[Explore your treatment options](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/treatment-centre) · [See the SHIFT Programme](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/programme)

## Common questions

### Is the cheapest Wegovy provider necessarily unsafe?

No. Compare the registered provider, clinical assessment, pharmacy, total cost and support. A low price alone does not prove a medicine is fake, and a higher price does not guarantee better care.

### Does a four-week supply mean one calendar month?

No. Thirteen four-week supplies cover 52 weeks. Twelve cover 48 weeks. Check the supply period and payment schedule before comparing quotes.

### Can I use my starting price to work out the full year?

Only if the same price and supply terms genuinely apply throughout. Dose changes, introductory offers and separate fees can change the total. Ask for the later prices before committing.

### Do I have to buy medication through SHIFT to use its information?

No. The public Knowledge guides are there to help you understand your options. You can also explore the Programme and its membership terms if you want practical support alongside treatment obtained elsewhere or without medication.

### What if I am thinking about stopping treatment?

Discuss it with your prescriber and ask about the next stage of support. SHIFT's [coming-off guide](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/stopping-glp1) can help you prepare questions and think about practical routines; it does not change your prescription.

## About the author

**Matt O’Brien · Founder, SHIFT Some Timber**

Matt O’Brien is the founder of SHIFT Some Timber, a men’s health business focused on practical support with weight, everyday habits and getting your life back.

rows.title: Oral semaglutide for weight loss in the UK: what 13.6% means
rows.author: Matt O’Brien
rows.summary: Oral semaglutide in the UK: understand the 64-week OASIS 4 result, prescription requirements, side effects and support beyond the tablet.
rows.body:
Is oral semaglutide approved in the UK?

Yes. The MHRA approved Wegovy tablets for weight management on 11 June 2026. The licence covers adults with a BMI of at least 30, or at least 27 with a weight-related condition, alongside diet and activity changes. A prescriber must assess suitability.

The approval announcement explicitly said the tablet was not then available through the NHS. A UK licence does not establish NHS funding, local access or stock at SHIFT. Check the current pathway with your clinician. Read the MHRA announcement.

What does 13.6% weight loss actually mean?

In OASIS 4, 307 adults without diabetes were allocated to oral semaglutide 25 mg or placebo. At week 64, estimated average body-weight change was −13.6% with semaglutide and −2.2% with placebo. These are trial averages, not a promise of your result, and body-weight loss is not the same as pure fat loss.

The trial compared the tablet with placebo, not directly with Mounjaro or a Wegovy injection. It cannot establish which option would work best for you. Gastrointestinal adverse events occurred in 74% of the semaglutide group and 42.2% of the placebo group. Read the original OASIS 4 study.

What is different about taking a tablet?

The approved daily dose starts at 1.5 mg and rises through 4 mg, 9 mg and 25 mg, spending at least a month at each level. Follow the prescription and leaflet; do not jump to the headline trial dose yourself.

The MHRA describes taking the tablet whole after at least eight hours without food, with a sip of water, then waiting at least 30 minutes before food or drink. Ask your pharmacist how other morning medicines fit around it. Official dosing information.

A tablet removes the injection, but adds a daily routine. Before choosing, think about your actual mornings: shifts, breakfast, school runs and other medicines. A treatment that looks convenient on paper still needs to fit your day.

Side effects and when to get help

Nausea, vomiting, constipation and diarrhoea are recognised side effects. Tell your prescriber about your medical history and every medicine or supplement you take. Semaglutide is not used during pregnancy or breastfeeding; discuss planned pregnancy with your clinician.

Seek urgent medical advice for severe, persistent abdominal pain, particularly if it reaches your back, sudden vision loss, or symptoms that leave you unable to keep fluids down. Call 999 for a serious allergic reaction with breathing difficulty or swelling of the throat or tongue. NHS semaglutide safety information.

This is not a complete safety checklist or a personal dosing plan. Use the leaflet supplied with your exact product and contact your prescriber or pharmacist about side effects and changes to treatment.

What should you check before paying?

Ask who assesses you, who prescribes and which registered pharmacy dispenses. Get the total price at later doses, any consultation or delivery charges, and the cancellation terms. Ask how you contact someone if side effects make treatment difficult.

Do not mistake an introductory price for the ongoing cost. Ask whether the quoted supply covers four weeks or a calendar month, and whether support is included. Our Wegovy cost guide explains the questions to ask.

SHIFT availability

No stock available today. This guide is information, not an offer to prescribe or dispense medication. Check the Treatment Centre for current product status and service details.

SHIFT’s take: plan for life around the treatment

The useful question is bigger than “pill or pen?” It is “what helps me keep going on an ordinary Tuesday?” Food you can manage, movement that fits, a place to check in, and someone qualified to contact about the prescription all matter.

SHIFT’s Programme brings practical food, movement and Life Back support together. You can explore it whether your medication comes from elsewhere, you are considering treatment, or you have stopped. Clinical decisions remain with your prescriber.

If you are thinking about stopping, use our coming-off guide to prepare for that conversation. If your provider has become hard to reach, Clinic Gone Quiet explains SHIFT’s support and its boundaries. We do not replace urgent care or your prescribing team.

Questions worth taking to your prescriber

  • Is this exact product suitable for my history and other medicines?
  • How should I fit it around breakfast and my normal routine?
  • Who do I contact between appointments, and when should I seek urgent help?
  • What happens if I cannot tolerate it, supply changes, or I want to stop?
  • What is included in the continuing cost?

You do not need to arrive with the right answers. You need a clear route to getting them.

About the author

Matt O’Brien · Founder, SHIFT Some Timber

Matt founded SHIFT to help ordinary men build practical routines around food, movement and getting their life back.

Sources and editorial note

By Matt O’Brien, founder of SHIFT Some Timber. Sources checked 20 September 2026. General information, not an individual treatment recommendation. No independent clinical review is claimed.

  • MHRA: Wegovy tablet approval, 11 June 2026
  • Wharton and colleagues: OASIS 4, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025
  • NHS: semaglutide

rows.title: NHS weight-loss medicines: who qualifies and what to ask
rows.author: SHIFT Team
rows.summary: Who may qualify for NHS weight-loss medicines, why access varies, and a practical checklist for asking your GP or local service about support.
rows.body:
**You may be able to get weight-loss medicine through the NHS, but there is no single UK eligibility rule.** The medicine, reason for treatment, health conditions, BMI and local service all matter. Meeting a published BMI threshold does not confirm that a prescription is suitable or available.

The useful first step is to ask your GP practice or local weight-management service **which assessment route is available and what help you can get now**. You can ask for weight-management support even if you do not qualify for a particular injection. The [NHS explains the wider support options](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/overweight-and-obesity/), including programmes, medicines and specialist assessment.

*Information checked on 5 October 2026. This is an editorial explanation of official guidance, not an individual assessment or an independent clinical review.*

## Why three different eligibility answers can all appear online

A medicine's **licence** describes its authorised use. A **NICE recommendation** describes the circumstances in which NHS use is recommended. **Commissioning and local delivery** concern the funded service, assessment route and implementation timetable. These are separate questions.

For example, [NICE TA1026](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026) recommends tirzepatide for weight management in adults with an initial BMI of at least 35 kg/m² and at least one weight-related condition, alongside dietary and activity support. Lower BMI thresholds, usually reduced by 2.5 kg/m², apply for specified ethnic backgrounds. England's primary-care rollout initially prioritises a narrower group.

That is why “NICE recommends it” and “your practice cannot currently offer it” can describe different parts of the pathway. Ask which rule is being applied, rather than assuming that one online calculator settles it.

## NHS weight-loss injections: the key distinctions

These are summaries of the **weight-management appraisals**, not a complete prescribing checklist or a promise of local availability.

| Medicine | Main distinction in NICE weight-management guidance |
|---|---|
| Tirzepatide, also called Mounjaro | TA1026: initial BMI at least 35 plus a weight-related condition; relevant ethnicity adjustments. England has phased primary-care access. |
| Semaglutide, also called Wegovy | TA875: a weight-related condition plus BMI at least 35, or BMI 30–34.9 with the specified specialist-referral criteria. Specialist provision and a maximum two-year course apply under this appraisal; relevant ethnicity adjustments apply. |
| Liraglutide, also called Saxenda | TA664: BMI at least 35, non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (raised blood sugar below the diabetes range) and high cardiovascular risk, through a specialist service; relevant lower BMI thresholds apply. |

Read the full [tirzepatide](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026), [semaglutide](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875) and [liraglutide](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta664) guidance for the conditions attached to each recommendation. These medicines are not the whole NHS pathway: [other options include orlistat and non-medicine support](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/overweight-and-obesity/).

**The reason for prescribing matters too.** Diabetes treatment has different criteria. There is also a separate [NICE semaglutide recommendation for cardiovascular risk reduction, TA1152](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1152), published in May 2026. Do not apply the TA875 weight-management restrictions to every possible semaglutide indication. Ask your clinician which guidance applies to your care.

## England: what the phased tirzepatide rollout means now

As checked on 5 October 2026, the published primary-care cohorts include:

| Access cohort | BMI before relevant ethnicity adjustment | Qualifying conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Cohort 1, introduced first | At least 40 | At least four of the five conditions below |
| Cohort 2, introduced from 23 June 2026 | 35–39.9 | At least four of the five conditions below |

The five conditions are type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnoea and dyslipidaemia (abnormal blood fats). The BMI adjustment is 2.5 kg/m² for people from South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean backgrounds. The service checks the applicable diagnostic definitions.

The [current NHS Cheshire and Merseyside patient guidance](https://cheshireandmerseyside.nhs.uk/your-health/prescribing/statements/mounjaro-tirzepatide/) sets out these cohorts and makes clear that practice participation and availability can vary. The [NHS England Digital cohort appendix](https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-collections-and-data-sets/data-collections/tirzepatide-in-primary-care-data-collection/prescribing-activity-of-tirzepatide-mounjaro-in-primary-care-settings/appendix) also distinguishes the rollout cohorts. Specialist-service access is a separate route; ask whether it applies to you.

Later expansion is planned, but a future cohort is not current eligibility. Check the [NHS England patient information](https://www.england.nhs.uk/ourwork/prevention/obesity/medicines-for-obesity/weight-management-injections/) and your local service when seeking an assessment.

## Your GP appointment checklist

You do not need to arrive knowing which medicine to request. Arrive ready to explain what is difficult and what you want help with.

**Prepare one short note:**

- Your recent weight history, if you have it. Bring accurate records rather than trying to adjust a number to fit an eligibility rule.
- Your diagnosed conditions, current medicines and supplements, and previous treatment or side effects.
- Support you have tried, what helped and what was difficult to maintain.
- The practical barriers: shifts, food costs, pain, low mood, family responsibilities or difficulty attending appointments.
- What better health would let you do: walk comfortably, manage work, sleep better or feel more confident.

A useful opening is: “I'd like help managing my weight. Can we review the support available and whether I need a specialist assessment?”

**Ask these five questions:**

1. Which weight-management service can assess me, and do I need a referral or can I refer myself?
2. If medicine is considered, which eligibility and local access rules apply now?
3. Who would prescribe and review it, and whom would I contact between appointments?
4. What dietary, activity or behavioural support comes with treatment, and what support can I get while waiting?
5. What happens if treatment is unsuitable, causes problems, does not help enough or ends?

Before leaving, ask for the next action, who is responsible and when to check back. “Wait for contact” is easier to manage when you know which service will contact you and how to follow up.

## Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland

England's cohort timetable is not a UK-wide rule.

- **Scotland:** use [NHS inform's weight-loss information](https://www.nhsinform.scot/healthy-living/weight-loss/) and ask your GP about your local health board's pathway.
- **Wales:** use [NHS 111 Wales information on obesity](https://111.wales.nhs.uk/Encyclopaedia/o/article/obesity/) and ask your GP or local health board which weight-management service is available.
- **Northern Ireland:** [nidirect's current weight-management services page](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/weight-management-services) explains developing services and local access. Ask your GP or Health and Social Care Trust about the appropriate route.

A medicine recommendation in another nation does not establish your local access.

## If the answer is “not currently available”

Ask what the reason is: clinical suitability, current rollout criteria, referral requirements or service availability. Then ask what support can be offered instead and whether circumstances that affect access will be reviewed.

The [NHS lists options for finding local support](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/overweight-and-obesity/), including checking your practice website and, in England, your Integrated Care Board website. Some programmes accept self-referrals. [NHS Better Health](https://www.nhs.uk/better-health/lose-weight/) also provides free resources.

Pick a manageable starting point, such as planning one regular meal, and discuss activity suited to your health. Avoid extreme restriction while waiting. If low mood, pain or eating difficulties are part of the problem, say so: support should take the whole situation into account.

Private treatment does not automatically transfer to the NHS. If you already have a prescriber, ask about transfer arrangements before ending that care and bring your treatment records.

## Common questions

### Can my GP prescribe a weight-loss injection?

Some tirzepatide weight-management prescribing is delivered through primary care in England. Your practice must confirm its arrangements and assess suitability. Other routes may involve specialist services.

### Is BMI 35 enough to qualify?

No. The medicine's recommendation, related conditions, treatment indication, relevant ethnicity adjustment and current service pathway all matter.

### Can I still ask for help if I do not qualify?

Yes. Ask about weight-management programmes, practical support and assessment of conditions that make weight difficult to manage. An injection threshold is not a threshold for deserving help.

For a broader explanation of routes, see our [NHS weight-loss medication pathways guide](/guides/nhs-weight-loss-medication-pathways). For your next appointment, use the checklist above and confirm one clear next step.

*Editorial update — 5 October 2026: the original publication date is retained. This revision clarifies current access cohorts, separates treatment indications and adds an appointment checklist and national information routes. It does not certify individual eligibility.*

rows.summary: Understand the limits of body-composition claims and prepare useful questions about nutrition, suitable strength activity and monitoring.
rows.body:
# Weight-loss medicines and muscle: what to ask about strength and nutrition

A falling weight does not tell you how much change came from fat, muscle, fluid or other tissue. Research on body composition needs careful interpretation, and one trial average cannot predict the amount of muscle an individual man will lose.

## Lean mass is not the same measurement as muscle

Body-composition studies often report lean mass or fat-free mass. These measures include more than skeletal muscle. They are not a direct measure of strength, function or whether somebody can carry shopping, climb stairs or get up from a chair.

Study populations, methods, medicine doses and follow-up periods differ. A headline that promises to prevent muscle loss, or applies a single kilogram average to UK men generally, goes further than those measurements support. This page makes neither claim.

## Discuss nutrition before choosing a target

If appetite or intake has changed during treatment, tell the prescribing service what you can actually eat. Ask whether you need support from a registered dietitian. A protein calculator is an estimate, not an individual prescription, particularly where kidney disease, other conditions or a restricted diet affect what is suitable.

Prepare a few practical details: the meals you usually manage, foods you avoid, your budget, cooking facilities and any nausea or swallowing difficulty. Do not assume a supplement solves inadequate overall intake. If you are unable to eat or drink adequately, obtain medical advice rather than relying on this article.

## Keep movement appropriate to your starting point

Strength activities can form part of an ordinary activity plan. The NHS provides beginner strength guidance with supported versions of movements. Choose suitable activity and build gradually; existing pain, balance difficulties or medical conditions may require individual advice.

- Ask which movements and amount are appropriate for you.
- Learn the technique from a reputable guide or qualified professional.
- Notice recovery and symptoms as well as repetitions or weight lifted.
- Include activities you want to do in daily life when discussing progress.
- Avoid using a generic programme as proof that a particular exercise is safe for you.

No exercise plan can guarantee preservation of every kilogram of lean tissue. Do not push through concerning symptoms to satisfy a target.

## Questions for your next review

What should we monitor alongside body weight? Is the rate of change appropriate for my circumstances? Does my food intake need assessment? Would a dietitian, physiotherapist or qualified exercise professional help? When should I seek advice rather than wait for the next appointment?

If a home scale reports a muscle percentage, ask how that estimate is obtained and how to interpret it. Do not change a prescribed medicine because one reading moved.

## What My Timber can help with

Grub and Fit can help organise everyday food and movement choices. They do not provide body-composition assessment, clinical monitoring or a promise to prevent treatment-related muscle loss. Your prescriber remains responsible for treatment decisions. SHIFT medicine ordering remains closed while the regulated partner is not commissioned.

## Sources and editorial note

- [NHS: strength exercises](https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/strength-exercises/).
- [NHS: eating a balanced diet, including individual dietary needs](https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/how-to-eat-a-balanced-diet/eating-a-balanced-diet/).
- [Wegovy: current UK product information](https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/13800/smpc).

Editorial correction: 2 October 2026. The unsupported universal 1.74 kg headline and prevention promise have been removed. General information; independent clinical or trainer review is not claimed.

# GLP-1 and exercise: strength, movement and safety

![GLP-1 exercise strength title card](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1790267969717_GLP-1-exercise-strength-title-card.jpeg)

Activity can support health and day-to-day strength during GLP-1 treatment. The useful starting point is a plan matched to your fitness, mobility, symptoms and medical conditions. General exercise targets are goals to work towards, not a requirement to train through illness or a test of whether you deserve treatment. This guide separates what studies show from practical options to discuss with your care team.

***

> **Key points**
>
> - Include strength and aerobic activity in a way that suits your ability and health.
> - Build gradually; rest and clinical advice take priority when you are unwell.
> - Food intake and protein needs deserve attention when appetite falls.
> - Lean mass is not the same measurement as muscle strength.
> - A coach can help with routines; medicine changes and symptom assessment belong with a clinician.

***

## What trials and UK guidance say about GLP-1 and exercise

Wegovy and Mounjaro are licensed for weight management alongside diet and activity measures. That does not establish a minimum exercise quota for every patient or mean the medicine cannot act in someone with limited mobility. Ask your prescriber how the advice applies to disability, pain, fatigue or other conditions. An achievable activity plan should fit the person receiving treatment.

Medicine trials often include lifestyle counselling in both treatment and comparison groups. Their results therefore describe the intervention that was studied; they do not isolate the effect of a particular gym routine. Evidence for one medicine and exercise programme should not be turned into a promise about every GLP-1 product.

The [SEMALEAN study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41068996/) observed changes in body composition and function during semaglutide treatment. Its findings should be read as observational evidence, not proof that a specific exercise programme prevented muscle loss. Lean mass includes tissues and water beyond skeletal muscle. A change on a body-composition scan and a change in strength are related questions, but they are not interchangeable.

Reviews discuss nutrition, resistance exercise and monitoring as possible ways to support muscle health. A review is a synthesis of evidence and expert interpretation; it does not make one routine compulsory or establish that everyone can prevent all lean-tissue loss.

**Useful topics to cover with your care team:**

- Whether you are eating enough overall and need individual dietary advice
- Strength activities that suit your joints, balance and experience
- Changes in everyday tasks, such as getting up from a chair
- Symptoms or loss of function that need assessment rather than harder training

> **Keep the evidence in proportion:** the [review of muscle-preservation strategies](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42346344/) discusses combined approaches. It is not a trial proving a particular programme works for every medicine or every patient.

The [NHS adult activity guidance](https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/physical-activity-guidelines-for-adults-aged-19-to-64/) gives general weekly targets, including strengthening major muscle groups on at least two days. These are population guidelines, not a GLP-1-specific prescription. If you have been inactive or have health concerns, discuss an appropriate starting point before increasing intensity.

## How should you programme strength, cardio and balance work?

Start with what you can do comfortably and repeat. You can build a routine around walking, adapted seated movement, resistance bands or gym equipment. There is no need to introduce every element at once, and a plan should allow for pain, disability, work patterns and recovery.

**1. Strength activities suited to your starting point.** Examples include supported sit-to-stands, wall press-ups and a resistance-band row. Ask a qualified exercise professional or physiotherapist for help with technique or adaptations if needed. Begin with a manageable amount rather than copying a demanding set-and-repetition target. Increase difficulty gradually only when the current activity feels comfortable and your health allows it. Stop a movement that causes concerning pain.

**2. Aerobic activity spread through the week.** The general adult target is 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity weekly, or an equivalent mix. Short sessions can contribute. Brisk walking, cycling and swimming are examples, but the best option is one you can access and tolerate. Build towards a suitable goal from your current level; vigorous exercise is not necessary to begin.

**3. Balance and functional training, especially if you're older or have been inactive for a while.** Simple exercises like sit-to-stands, single-leg balance holds, or step-ups build the kind of functional strength that keeps you steady and independent, not just strong on paper.

**4. Adapt to how you feel.** Mild symptoms may make a shorter or gentler session more comfortable, but resting is also reasonable. Do not train through vomiting, significant diarrhoea, dehydration, faintness or severe pain. Seek medical advice when symptoms persist or prevent normal eating or drinking. A missed workout is not a reason to change your medicine dose.

**Practical tip:** Keep a short-session option for days when you feel well enough to move but have less time. Keep a rest option too. Record troublesome symptoms separately so they reach your prescriber rather than being treated only as an exercise-planning problem.

If you want more detail on adapting training around side effects, our guide to exercise on GLP-1 treatment covers walking progressions and strength adaptations in more depth.

## How much protein do you need to protect muscle on GLP-1?

Reduced appetite can make it harder to eat enough. [Guy's and St Thomas' nutrition guidance](https://www.guysandstthomas.nhs.uk/health-information/lifestyle-advice-people-taking-weight-loss-medicines/food-and-nutrition) gives 80–100g protein daily as general-population advice and specifically directs people with chronic kidney disease to a dietitian for personalised targets. Your own needs depend on health, body size and intake; an online number should not override an agreed dietetic plan.

> **Make meals workable:** Include protein-containing foods you enjoy across the day, alongside other food groups. You do not need to force a fixed amount at each meal. If small portions repeatedly leave you unable to meet your needs, discuss that with your prescriber or dietitian.

There is no need to buy a supplement or organise every meal around a narrow workout window to use this guide. Focus first on a varied pattern you can tolerate. A dietitian can help if food restrictions, allergies, kidney disease, persistent nausea or low intake make that difficult.

**Practical tactics for low-appetite days:**

- Try smaller portions more often if large meals are difficult.
- Include foods such as eggs, beans, lentils, tofu, yoghurt, fish or poultry according to preference.
- Keep convenient foods available for days when cooking is difficult.
- Ask about an appropriate supplement if ordinary food is insufficient; do not assume a multivitamin corrects an inadequate diet.
- Seek advice if reduced intake is persistent or you feel weak or unwell.

Simple options include eggs on toast, lentil soup, yoghurt with fruit, beans with a baked potato, or fish with vegetables and a starchy food. Choose foods that suit your appetite and budget rather than trying to make every meal a high-protein product. The aim is nourishment and a routine you can manage. Persistent difficulty eating needs attention, even if the scales are falling.

## What does a realistic weekly training plan look like?

Here is an example of how a week could be organised. It is an adaptable planning example, not a prescription or a minimum amount everyone should complete. Choose activities and duration appropriate to your own health, and use a clinician's or physiotherapist's plan where you have one.

1. **Monday:** a short strength session using suitable movements.
2. **Tuesday:** a walk, cycle or adapted aerobic activity at a manageable pace.
3. **Wednesday:** rest, light movement or mobility work if comfortable.
4. **Thursday:** a second suitable strength session if recovered.
5. **Friday:** another short aerobic session if well enough.
6. **Saturday:** an enjoyable activity, such as walking with a friend or gardening.
7. **Sunday:** rest or light activity according to how you feel.

If equipment is unavailable, ask about safe bodyweight or band-based alternatives. If balance is uncertain, avoid unsupported movements that could lead to a fall. You can record duration, how hard an activity felt and symptoms afterwards. That gives you a useful basis for adapting the next week without judging success only by the number of sessions completed.

## Are there safety checks you need before training on GLP-1?

A few safety rules matter more than the rest, particularly if you're on other diabetes medication alongside a GLP-1.

- **Insulin or sulfonylureas:** ask your diabetes team for an exercise and glucose-monitoring plan, including how to recognise and treat a hypo. Do not change doses yourself.
- **Severe, persistent abdominal pain:** seek urgent medical attention, especially if pain reaches your back or comes with vomiting.
- **Vomiting, diarrhoea or faintness:** pause exercise and seek advice if you cannot maintain fluids or symptoms persist.
- **Chest pain, collapse or severe breathing difficulty:** use emergency care, not an exercise review.
- **New weakness or loss of everyday function:** tell your clinician; a training log is useful but cannot diagnose the cause.

**Practical tip:** Write down what changed, when it began and whether it happens at rest as well as during activity. Do not wait for a routine appointment if symptoms are severe, sudden or worsening.

For more detail on managing nausea, constipation and when symptoms cross the line into needing help, see our guide on GLP-1 side effects.

## Does age or diabetes change how you should train on GLP-1?

Not everyone starting a GLP-1 medicine is starting from the same place, and the guidance should flex accordingly.

**Older adults** may benefit from particular attention to balance, strength and activities needed for daily living. Age alone does not determine what someone can safely lift. Falls history, frailty, pain and previous experience matter. A physiotherapist or suitably qualified professional can help you choose safe movements and a progression you can manage.

![Older man practising a sit-to-stand](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1790267908312_Older-man-practising-a-sit-to-stand.jpeg)

**People with type 2 diabetes** should follow their diabetes team's advice about activity, meals and glucose checks. Monitoring needs differ, especially when insulin or a sulfonylurea is used. Bring the full medicine list to both teams if your weight-management and diabetes care are provided separately.

**After inactivity or surgery**, follow any recovery restrictions and start at a suitable level. A recent operation needs the surgical team's advice; a generic ten-minute walk is not appropriate for every recovery. Tell the anaesthetic team about GLP-1 treatment before a planned procedure and follow their instructions about medicines and fasting.

If any of this feels beyond what you can safely self-manage, a formal exercise prescription or physiotherapy referral is a reasonable ask of your GP or prescriber.

## What happens to muscle and fitness over months on GLP-1?

Changes in weight, body composition and function do not follow a single timetable. SEMALEAN reported group-level observations over follow-up; it cannot tell an individual when their strength will improve. Notice everyday changes such as stairs becoming easier or harder, but seek advice about unexplained weakness rather than assuming it is an expected phase.

Review a routine according to your own progress. You might need to reduce difficulty, change an exercise, improve access to food or get help with symptoms. Increasing training every week is not the only sign of progress. Being able to carry out daily tasks comfortably and safely is a useful goal in its own right.

If treatment is ending, discuss follow-up with the prescribing team. Weight regain can occur despite continued effort; exercise cannot guarantee prevention. Keep enjoyable, manageable activity in the plan and agree how concerns will be reviewed. There is no universal three-, six- or twelve-month exercise timetable that replaces individual follow-up.

## How does structured clinical support help you train safely on GLP-1?

Ask who is responsible for each part of your care. A prescriber assesses medicine suitability and symptoms; a dietitian can advise on clinical nutrition needs; an appropriately qualified exercise professional can help with activity within their competence. A lifestyle programme may offer some of these services or none. Check the actual offer before assuming they are included.

Useful support should make responsibilities and contact routes clear. Ask how to raise a symptom, whether there is a response-time commitment and what to do outside opening hours. No coaching service or app should be used as an emergency service. You can compare [lifestyle support and medicine pathways](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/comparisons/universal/lifestyle-vs-mounjaro), while confirming clinical arrangements with your own provider.

## Sources

- [Lean mass and musculoskeletal preservation in GLP‑1‑based obesity treatment: nutrition, exercise, supplementation, and monitoring strategies (PubMed)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42346344/)
- [Impact of semaglutide on fat mass, lean mass and muscle function in patients with obesity: The SEMALEAN study (PubMed)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41068996/)
- [Food and nutrition advice for people taking weight‑loss medicines (Guys and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust)](https://www.guysandstthomas.nhs.uk/health-information/lifestyle-advice-people-taking-weight-loss-medicines/food-and-nutrition)

This article is general information, not a substitute for advice from a qualified doctor. Consult a qualified healthcare professional about your own circumstances before acting on anything here.

## FAQ

### Is it okay to work out while taking a GLP-1 medicine?

Many people can be active during treatment, but the safe type and intensity depend on health and symptoms. Start at an appropriate level and seek advice if you have concerns. A medicine licence does not mean every workout is safe for every patient.

### Can you build muscle while on a GLP-1?

Strength and muscle mass are different outcomes. Appropriate training may support function, but results depend on many factors and cannot be guaranteed. If you are becoming weaker or struggling with daily tasks, ask for assessment rather than simply increasing training.

### Is walking enough exercise on GLP-1?

Walking can be a useful starting point. General activity guidance also includes strength work, adapted to your ability. Ask about alternatives if pain, disability or balance difficulties limit particular movements.

### Will GLP-1 work without exercise?

Medicine effects are not conditional on completing a fixed exercise quota. Activity has health benefits and is part of the wider treatment approach, but should be adapted to your circumstances. Discuss limitations with your prescriber rather than withholding or changing treatment yourself.

### How much protein should you eat on a GLP-1 medicine?

There is no single target for everyone. Discuss your intake if appetite is low, and seek personalised advice where you have kidney disease or other dietary needs. Food examples earlier in this guide are starting points, not a prescribed meal plan.

## Recommended

- [Muscle Loss on GLP-1 Treatment: What Men Can Do](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/muscle-on-glp1)
- [Exercise on GLP-1 Treatment: Walking, Strength and Safety](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/exercise-on-glp1)
- [Stopping GLP-1 Treatment | Weight Regain & Appetite](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/stopping-glp1)
- [GLP-1 Side Effects: Nausea, Constipation and When to Get Help](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/glp1-side-effects)

## What My Timber can help with

Record the movement you actually managed and how you felt afterwards. Take questions about symptoms, treatment and safe exercise limits to your clinician; a general activity plan cannot answer those clinical questions.

My Timber provides everyday support with food, movement, personal goals and progress records. It does not prescribe medicines, decide doses or provide a clinical review. Medicine assessment, prescribing, dispensing and treatment monitoring belong with your appropriately regulated healthcare provider.

# Wegovy not working? Preparing for a treatment review

![Decorative Wegovy weight stall title card](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1790385228551_Decorative-Wegovy-weight-stall-title-card.jpeg)

If your weight is not changing as expected on Wegovy, arrange a review rather than assuming you have failed. Response, prescribed treatment, tolerability and other health factors all deserve consideration. There is no blanket instruction to wait 16–20 weeks or to continue through concerning symptoms. This guide helps you prepare useful information for your prescriber; it does not set a dose or switching plan.

***

> **Key points**
>
> - Slow progress has several possible explanations and cannot be diagnosed from a weight chart alone.
> - Review the exact product and prescribed schedule with your care team.
> - Report troublesome symptoms promptly; urgent symptoms need urgent care.
> - Tests should be chosen for your circumstances, not ordered as a universal checklist.
> - Do not increase, restart or switch treatment using an article.

***

## Common reasons Wegovy may not appear to be working

A review should consider both the treatment and your experience without assuming poor effort or incorrect use. Some people respond less than others even when they follow the plan. It helps to bring reliable records and specific questions rather than trying to identify a single cause yourself.

If treatment is still being adjusted, tell the prescriber exactly what you have taken and for how long. A dose-escalation schedule is intended to manage treatment safely; it is not a promise that appetite or weight will change only after a particular step. You can ask for advice before the end of titration.

Food and activity form part of weight-management care, but a plateau alone does not prove excess eating. Discuss appetite, access to food, symptoms and what is practical in your routine. An honest account is more useful than a stricter diet adopted just before the appointment. If intake is already low, further restriction may be inappropriate.

Ask a pharmacist or prescriber to check administration and storage if you are unsure. Bring the exact product name and instructions. Mention missed doses or supply gaps without embarrassment; this helps them advise safely. Do not take extra doses to make up for a perceived lack of effect.

Topics worth reviewing include:

- **Treatment history:** prescribed doses, interruptions and administration questions.
- **Tolerability:** symptoms, low intake or difficulty drinking.
- **Weight trend:** the length of the apparent plateau and how readings were taken.
- **Other health factors:** new symptoms, diagnoses or medicine changes.
- **Expectations:** whether the goal and review schedule remain appropriate.

Plateaus in particular can feel like failure when they're often just the body adjusting. It's worth reading about how to [check before panicking about a plateau](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/weight-loss-plateau-men) rather than assuming the treatment has stopped working altogether.

**Pro Tip:** *Keep a simple weekly log of your dose, injection day, and roughly what you've eaten. It takes two minutes and gives your clinician something concrete to work from at your next review.*

## How Wegovy dosing and timing affect results

Wegovy's dosing schedule is deliberately slow, and that's often the first thing worth checking if results seem disappointing.

The current UK injection instructions use gradual dose escalation, but Wegovy formulations and available doses are not interchangeable. Follow your own prescription and product leaflet. An older graphic showing a single 16–20-week route should not be used to choose a dose. Ask your prescriber what applies to the product you actually receive.

Clinical trials measure group outcomes over defined periods. The [STEP 3 trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33625476/) studied weekly semaglutide with intensive behavioural therapy; it does not establish a personal result or a date before which concerns should be ignored. Comparing your first few weeks with a trial's final average can create an unrealistic expectation.

Useful questions about the schedule include:

- What is my prescribed plan and next review date?
- What should I do if I cannot tolerate the current treatment?
- Who should advise me after an interruption or supply gap?
- Which symptoms mean I need urgent help?

A review can happen whenever there is a concern. Do not wait for maintenance or a fixed number of weeks to report symptoms or discuss a lack of progress.

## How side effects and tolerability can reduce effectiveness

Tolerability is part of whether treatment is suitable. A lower scale reading is not a good outcome if you cannot eat or drink adequately. Your prescriber may need to reconsider the plan; an article cannot determine the right change.

Digestive symptoms are recognised in the UK product information. Tell the service how severe they are, how long they last and what you can manage to eat and drink. This is more useful than describing every symptom as normal titration.

Do not push through severe symptoms to reach a higher dose. Nor should a coach or app advise you to change doses. Get appropriate clinical advice.

Not all symptoms are equal, though. [MHRA guidance for GLP-1 prescribers](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/mhra-updates-guidance-for-glp-1-prescribers-and-patients) flags severe abdominal pain as a red flag that needs urgent medical assessment, since it can indicate pancreatitis rather than routine gastrointestinal upset.

For mild symptoms, ask the prescribing team about practical food and fluid measures appropriate to you. If you cannot keep fluids down, symptoms persist or you feel unwell, seek medical advice rather than relying on self-care. Sudden vision loss also needs urgent assessment.

![Small balanced meal beside a glass of water](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1790385228240_Small-balanced-meal-beside-a-glass-of-water.jpeg)

**Pro Tip:** *If nausea is putting you off food entirely rather than just reducing appetite, tell your prescriber. That's a sign to adjust the approach, not just tough it out.*

## Medical checks and investigations to consider if weight loss stalls

A clinician can consider whether a condition or another medicine is relevant to the change in weight. A plateau does not diagnose a thyroid problem, diabetes or an interaction. Bring new symptoms and medicine changes to the review rather than requesting the same panel of tests for everyone.

Some treatments and health conditions can affect weight, but do not stop a medicine prescribed for another condition. Ask the prescriber to review the whole list, including non-prescription products. If a test is suggested, ask what question it is intended to answer and how the result would change care.

A useful review checklist is:

- Review symptoms, medical history and the complete medicine list.
- Decide whether any tests are indicated for the individual circumstances.
- Remember that HbA1c assesses longer-term blood glucose; it is not a direct test for insulin resistance.
- Discuss whether specialist input would help and how a referral would work.

[NICE TA875](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875/chapter/1-recommendations) sets conditions for NHS use, including specialist-service provision. Those commissioning criteria should not be presented as the licensing conditions for every private prescription. Ask your own service which clinical and funding rules apply.

## Practical steps to improve response while staying safe

While waiting for a routine review, keep the plan manageable. These are options to discuss, not a promise that changing habits will overcome an inadequate medicine response:

1. **Keep meals workable:** record appetite and difficulties rather than automatically eating less.
2. **Choose suitable movement:** adapt activity to your ability and symptoms.
3. **Note sleep and stress:** mention persistent problems if they affect daily life.
4. **Describe alcohol and other products honestly:** include supplements and non-prescription medicines.
5. **Keep treatment records:** note prescribed doses, interruptions and questions for the pharmacist or prescriber.

The [NHS's calorie counting guidance](https://www.nhs.uk/better-health/lose-weight/calorie-counting/) is a solid, free starting point for structuring meals around a sensible deficit.

**Pro Tip:** *Pick one change from this list to focus on for a fortnight rather than trying to overhaul everything at once. Consistency beats intensity.*

Support should address practical barriers without blaming you for the outcome. Check which parts are clinical care and which are general coaching. Neither a programme nor a tracking tool can guarantee weight loss or replace an individual treatment decision.

## Clinical stopping rules, treatment duration and what happens if you stop or switch

Treatment needs review with your prescriber. The [current UK Wegovy product information](https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/13800/smpc) says that, if weight loss is below 5% of starting weight after six months of treatment, the clinician needs to decide whether to continue after considering individual benefits and risks. This is six months on treatment, not six months after reaching a maintenance dose. NHS funding and service criteria are a separate question: check the current pathway with the service responsible for your care. Do not stop, increase or restart treatment using this article.

Stopping isn't necessarily the end of the story, though. Evidence from a withdrawal trial found that continuing semaglutide maintained further weight loss, while switching to placebo led to significant regain, with a statistically significant difference between groups over 48 weeks, according to [trial data on maintenance of weight loss](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33755728/). That's a strong signal that whatever weight loss you achieve on Wegovy tends to need an ongoing plan, whether that's continued medication, a structured maintenance approach, or both.

Key points to raise at a review:

- **Ask what your 6-month checkpoint result was** and what it means for continuing.
- **Agree a stopping or switching plan with your prescriber** if treatment is ending; this article does not provide a taper or restart schedule.
- **Plan for maintenance before you stop**, not after.

## Sources

- [Effect of Continued Once-Weekly Subcutaneous Semaglutide on Maintenance of Weight Loss in Adults With Overweight or Obesity](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33755728/)
- [Semaglutide for managing overweight and obesity (NICE TA875)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta875/chapter/1-recommendations)
- [Wegovy: EPAR — public assessment report (European Medicines Agency)](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/assessment-report/wegovy-epar-public-assessment-report_en.pdf)
- [MHRA updates guidance for GLP-1 prescribers and patients](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/mhra-updates-guidance-for-glp-1-prescribers-and-patients)

## FAQ

### Why am I not responding to Wegovy?

There are several possible explanations, including variation in response. Bring your treatment history, weight records and symptoms to a review. Do not assume that a slow result proves poor adherence or that a higher dose is the answer.

### How can I speed up weight loss on Wegovy?

Do not try to accelerate treatment by increasing doses, combining medicines or severely restricting food. Discuss whether the goal and plan remain appropriate. Safe care matters more than matching someone else's rate of loss.

### Why am I not losing anything on Wegovy?

A review can consider the exact medicine, treatment exposure, symptoms and relevant health factors. You do not need to wait until a particular week to ask for help, and no single online checklist can identify the cause.

### Why is Wegovy taking so long to work?

Titration and response vary, but a slow result should not be dismissed automatically. Ask your prescribing service when and how to assess benefit. The injection schedule and a trial's endpoint are different from your personal review needs.

## Recommended

- [Wegovy side effects and red flags](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/articles/wegovy-side-effects-timeline)
- [Wegovy vs orlistat](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/comparisons/medications/wegovy-vs-orlistat)
- [Wegovy injection and tablets](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/comparisons/medications/wegovy-injection-vs-tablets)
- [Wegovy vs Saxenda](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/comparisons/medications/wegovy-vs-saxenda)

## What My Timber can help with

Prepare your dose history, missed doses, symptoms and weight records for a review with your own prescriber. Do not increase, restart or switch medicine on the basis of an online article.

My Timber provides everyday support with food, movement, personal goals and progress records. It does not prescribe medicines, decide doses or provide a clinical review. Medicine assessment, prescribing, dispensing and treatment monitoring belong with your appropriately regulated healthcare provider.

We removed unsupported descriptions of SHIFT clinical services and unapproved personal attribution where present. This correction does not represent an independent clinical review of the whole article.

# Binge eating and weight-loss medicines: keep the treatment questions separate

Repeated episodes of eating with a sense of losing control deserve appropriate support. They are not something you have to solve by being stricter, and a weight-loss medicine is not automatically a treatment for an eating disorder.

## Start with an assessment, not a medicine recommendation

Tell a GP or appropriate healthcare professional what happens, how often, how you feel afterwards and how it affects your life. You do not need to prove that your weight is high enough or that the episodes are severe enough to ask for help.

Eating-disorder care needs to consider the whole situation, including mental and physical health. A diagnosis cannot be made from a calorie log, an online quiz or a coaching conversation. If you have already been prescribed a medicine for another purpose, tell the clinician assessing your eating difficulties about it.

## What established guidance says

NICE recommends eating-disorder-focused support for binge eating disorder, starting with guided self-help where appropriate and considering further psychological treatment according to the person's needs. It advises against medication as the sole treatment for binge eating disorder.

The NHS explains that trying to diet during treatment can make it harder to stop binge eating. Discuss food changes and any weight-management treatment with the team looking after you rather than combining conflicting plans yourself.

## Research is not an individual treatment recommendation

Interest in how GLP-1 medicines affect appetite does not establish that any particular medicine is an approved or suitable treatment for your eating disorder. A small or early study is not equivalent to a large controlled trial, a licence or an individual assessment. This article does not recommend starting, stopping or changing a medicine to manage binge eating.

If you are considering a study or a proposed off-label treatment, ask the clinician what evidence supports it, what uncertainty remains, how safety is monitored and what established options are available. Do not buy a medicine without a legitimate prescription or use a product sold as a research peptide.

## Prepare for the conversation

- Describe the episodes in your own words, including the sense of control and the distress involved.
- Mention restriction, fasting, vomiting, laxative use or excessive exercise if these occur.
- Bring your medicine list and tell the clinician about other health conditions.
- Ask how to obtain eating-disorder support locally and what to do while waiting.
- Say if tracking food, weight or calories makes the difficulty worse.

These notes are preparation for care, not a checklist you must complete before receiving help. Seek urgent medical help for an immediate safety concern rather than waiting to build a diary.

## Where SHIFT fits

My Timber can organise everyday goals if that is useful to you. It is not an eating-disorder treatment, symptom assessment or monitored clinical service. You can pause tracking that is unhelpful and seek appropriate care independently of a SHIFT purchase. SHIFT medicine ordering remains closed while the regulated partner is not commissioned.
